question.leadin: This city was the projected destination of a 1965 protest march that began in Selma.
question.text: Name this Alabama capital, the site of a bus boycott that began in 1955.
question.clue: This city was the destination of a march, whose participants were attacked by police on "Bloody Sunday" while crossing the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma.

swap.leadin: This Supreme Court case overturned the "separate but equal" doctrine of Plessy v. Ferguson.
swap.text: Name this case, in which the Court unanimously ruled that segregation in schools was unconstitutional.
swap.clue: This case's decision cited an experiment in which children were asked to choose between dolls by Kenneth and Mamie Clark.

question.text: As president, Johnson launched this series of programs that included Medicare and Medicaid. Its most famous part was the "War on Poverty" that led to the Economic Opportunity Act.
question.clue: Largely overseen by Bill Moyers and Richard Goodwin, it also saw the creation of the National Endowment for the Arts, and was originally outlined during a commencement speech at the University of Michigan.

swap.leadin: This man declared "segregation now, segregation tomorrow, segregation forever," then tried to back that up by standing in the door to block two black students from entering his state's university in Tuscaloosa.
swap.text: Name this politician. His wife, Lurleen, ran for governor when he was term-limited in 1966.
swap.clue: This man considered Colonel Sanders as a running mate for one campaign, but ultimately chose nuclear weapons enthusiast Curtis Lemay.

question.text: Name this president who created Medicare and Medicaid through his Great Society program as part of his war on poverty.
question.clue: This man ironically formed the "Stop Kennedy" coalition in 1960 with Adlai Stevenson and Hubert Humphrey.

swap.text: This FBI program was created to covertly infiltrate and disrupt groups such as the American Indian Movement and also targeted Martin Luther King, Jr.
swap.clue: This program included Operation Hoodwink, which attempted to drive wedges between Mafia bosses and the Communist Party.

question.leadin: This man outed Oliver Sipple, who had saved the life of Gerald Ford, in an attempt to dispel the stereotype that homosexuals were "timid, weak and unheroic figures."
question.text: Name this "Mayor of Castro Street," one of the first openly gay men to be elected to public office in the United States.
question.clue: This man's death inspired Cleve Jones to begin the NAMES Project.

swap.leadin: One member of this group, Melba Beals, published the book Warriors Don't Cry about her experiences attending Central High School.
swap.text: Name this group of African American students who attempted to transfer to an all-white high school in 1957 accompanied by the 101st Airborne Division.
swap.clue: Minnijean Brown was expelled after confrontations with other students, while Ernest Green, Jefferson Thomas, and Carlotta Walls Lanier graduated.

question.leadin: Former FCC commissioner Benjamin Hooks succeeded this man at his most prominent post, in 1977.
question.text: Name this St. Louis-born leader of the NAACP, who served as that organization's executive director throughout the height of the civil rights movement, beginning in 1955.
question.clue: This executive director of the NAACP refused to allow any public recognition for activist Bayard Rustin, probably because of Rustin's suspected homosexuality. This University of Minnesota graduate had previously replaced W.E.B. DuBois as editor of the magazine Crisis.

swap.leadin: The police in this case had received a tip that racketeer Virgil Ogletree was in a certain house, but failed to produce a search warrant.
swap.text: Name this supreme court case which arose after the plaintiff was convicted of pornography charges despite the police lacking probable cause to search her house.
swap.clue: Justice Harlan's dissent claimed that there was no reason to reconsider the case of Wolf v. Colorado, while the majority opinion for this case was written by Thomas Clark.

question.text: This Supreme Court Justice was a failed LBJ nominee to replace Earl Warren as Chief Justice. Defeated by a filibuster, this man later resigned from the Court completely in 1969 after an ethics scandal. This man previously represented Clarence Gideon in a Court case involving right to counsel.
question.clue: When Lyndon Johnson tried to elevate him to Chief Justice, a filibuster by a bipartisan coalition in the Senate forced the President to withdraw his nomination. He later resigned from the Court after a financial scandal.

swap.text: Hampton chaired the Illinois chapter of this revolutionary group founded by Bobby Seale and Huey Newton in Oakland. Richard Aoki, a leader of this group, was an FBI informant.
swap.clue: The Free Breakfast for Children program was founded by that U.S. group of this name, which was targeted by the Mulford Act to discourage its members' armed patrols of Oakland, which they called "copwatching."

question.text: This Baptist minister led protests after the Diallou shootings. This MSNBC commentator ran in the 2004 Democratic Primary, memorably asking Howard Dean in a debate whether he employed Black people on his staff.

swap.leadin: This work responded to an open letter penned by eight clergymen titled "A Call for Unity," which cautioned against "outsiders coming in."
swap.text: Name this text, which draws on Augustine in arguing that "injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere."
swap.answerHtml: “Letter from Birmingham Jail” [or “Letter from a Birmingham Jail” or “Letter from Birmingham City Jail” or “The Negro is Your Brother”]
swap.clue: It was written in response to the statement "A Call for Unity" that urged the use of the court system rather than "direct action" led by outsiders.

question.text: The exclusion of women at the march was protested by this African-American feminist, who had been arrested in 1970 for purchasing a shotgun used in an escape attempt by the Soledad Brothers, though she was acquitted.
question.clue: This former UCLA professor and member of the Black Panthers was put on trial for her alleged role in the attempted kidnapping of Judge Howard Haley at a Marin County courthouse.

swap.text: The Black Panther leader Eldridge Cleaver wrote this essay collection while in prison. This collection includes an allegorical reading of a Muhammad Ali fight in the context of black liberation as well as controversial homophobic and misogynist passages in its section "The Blood of the Beast."
swap.clue: Eldridge Cleaver wrote this memoir about American racism that denounces the "omnipotent administrators" and accuses James Baldwin of hating black people.

question.text: The Green Book helped develop this network of theaters and nightclubs catering to black audiences in the South. Similar to the Jewish Borscht Belt, it launched the careers of B.B. King, Ray Charles, and Marvin Gaye.
question.clue: During Jim Crow, black performers traveled to nightclubs such as the Uptown Theatre in Philadelphia that were part of this informal set of venues, whose name is a play on the Borscht Belt.

swap.text: This five-term Democratic Senator won fifteen electoral votes on an independent anti-civil rights plank in the 1960 Presidential election. His "machine" controlled the state for the last forty years of segregation, and his son of the same name later won a Virginia Senate seat as an independent.
swap.clue: This Virginia senator promised "massive resistance" in the face of Brown v. Board of Ed. His namesake organization dominated Virginia politics for much of the early to mid-20th century.

question.text: The issue of states ignoring Supreme Court decisions rose again in this unanimous 1958 decision, which arose out of Arkansas and held that states cannot choose to ignore the Court.

swap.leadin: This man pressured Bayard Rustin into resigning from the SCLC.
swap.text: Name this man who was a longtime Congressman representing Harlem. Due to accusations of impropriety, he was eventually stripped of his committee chairmanships and excluded by the House in 1967.
swap.clue: This Congressman, who was nicknamed "Mr. Civil Rights," was succeeded by Charlie Rangel in a post he held from 1945 to 1971.
